subChunks.title: Grid Layout
subChunks.hookHtml: Flexbox is brilliant for a single row of nav links. It breaks down the moment you need both rows and columns simultaneously. CSS Grid is the two-dimensional layout system every front-end developer reaches for when building real pages — and Tailwind puts it directly in your class string.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grid vs Flex — choosing the right tool

The rule of thumb is simple but important:

  • One axis (a row OR a column) → use flex
  • Two axes (rows AND columns simultaneously) → use grid

A navigation bar is one axis — items flow in a single row. Use flex. A feature card grid is two axes — you care about both the columns and the rows they fill. Use grid.

Basic grid setup

class="grid grid-cols-3 gap-6"

grid enables the grid context. grid-cols-3 creates three equal-width columns (1fr 1fr 1fr under the hood). gap-6 adds spacing between all cells.

Available column counts out of the box: grid-cols-1 through grid-cols-12. There is also grid-cols-none to reset.

Arbitrary column definitions — the sidebar pattern

The most useful real-world grid is a sidebar + main layout. You want the sidebar to be a fixed pixel width and the main area to consume the rest. Tailwind's arbitrary value syntax handles this perfectly:

class="grid grid-cols-[240px_1fr] gap-0"

Square brackets let you write any valid CSS value. 240px_1fr becomes 240px 1fr in the generated CSS — the underscores are spaces. This is one of the most commonly used arbitrary values in production Tailwind codebases.

Spanning columns and rows

col-span-2      /* stretch across 2 columns */
col-span-full   /* stretch to fill all columns */
col-start-2     /* start at column line 2 */
col-end-4       /* end before column line 4 */
row-span-2      /* stretch across 2 rows */

A hero card in a card grid that should span the full width? col-span-full. A featured item in a 3-column grid that should be twice as wide? col-span-2.

Gap control

gap-4       /* uniform gap on both axes */
gap-x-6     /* horizontal gap only */
gap-y-2     /* vertical gap only */

Alignment utilities

place-items-center   /* align-items + justify-items both center */
place-content-center /* align-content + justify-content both center */
items-start          /* align items at the start of their grid area */
justify-items-end    /* push items to the right of their grid area */

place-items-center is the one-line trick to perfectly centre content inside every cell — very useful for icon grids.

Auto-placement and auto columns

grid-flow-col     /* lay items out across columns instead of rows */
auto-cols-fr      /* auto-created columns are each 1fr */
auto-cols-min     /* columns shrink to fit their content */

These are useful for horizontal scrolling galleries where you don't know how many items there are at build time.

Practical patterns in React/JSX

/* 3-column feature card grid */
<div className="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6">
  {features.map(f => <FeatureCard key={f.id} {...f} />)}
</div>

/* Sidebar + main layout */
<div className="grid grid-cols-[240px_1fr] min-h-screen">
  <aside className="border-r border-gray-200">...</aside>
  <main className="p-8">...</main>
</div>

/* Asymmetric feature hero */
<div className="grid grid-cols-[1fr_2fr] gap-8 items-center">
  <div className="space-y-4">Copy...</div>
  <img className="rounded-xl" src="..." />
</div>

When NOT to use grid

Don't reach for grid for a row of buttons, a flex nav, or anything that genuinely only flows along one axis. Flex is simpler to reason about in those cases. The cognitive overhead of grid is worth it only when you're genuinely managing two dimensions.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain in your own words the difference between CSS Grid and Flexbox, and give a concrete example of a UI pattern where you would use each. Why doesn't flex work well for a card grid?

questions.questionHtml: Which Tailwind class creates a grid container with 3 equal columns?
questions.explanationHtml: You need both grid (sets display: grid) and grid-cols-3 (sets grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))). Neither alone is sufficient.

questions.questionHtml: You want a sidebar layout where the sidebar is exactly 256px wide and the main area fills remaining space. Which class value is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's arbitrary value syntax uses square brackets. Inside, spaces are represented as underscores: [256px_1fr] generates grid-template-columns: 256px 1fr.

questions.questionHtml: You have a 3-column card grid and want one card to stretch across all three columns. Which class do you add to that card?
questions.explanationHtml: col-span-full sets grid-column: 1 / -1, making the item span from the first to the last column line regardless of how many columns there are.

questions.questionHtml: A nav bar needs a logo on the left and links on the right, all vertically centred. Which layout tool and classes are most appropriate?
questions.explanationHtml: A nav bar is a single row — a one-dimensional layout. flex justify-between pushes the first and last children to opposite ends, and items-center vertically centres them. Grid would work but flex is simpler for a single axis.

questions.questionHtml: A junior developer builds a 3-column feature section using flex flex-wrap gap-6 and gives each card w-1/3. It mostly works — but cards in the last row don't align with those above, and on certain screen widths the third column wraps awkwardly. What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?
questions.correctAnswer: Flexbox doesn't enforce row alignment across multiple rows — wrapping items don't snap to a shared column grid. The fix is to switch to grid grid-cols-3 gap-6, which guarantees that all items align to the same column tracks regardless of content height.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the classic flex-wrap trap. flex-wrap with fractional widths is brittle — rounding errors cause gaps, and flex items in different rows don't share column tracks. CSS Grid solves both problems: items are placed on explicit tracks, so alignment is always consistent.

subChunks.title: Responsive Design
subChunks.hookHtml: More than half your users are on a phone. A design that only works at 1440px wide isn't a design — it's an accident. Tailwind's breakpoint system enforces mobile-first discipline: you write for the smallest screen first, then layer on larger-screen enhancements.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The mobile-first rule

In Tailwind, unprefixed utilities apply at all screen sizes. Breakpoint prefixes are minimum-width overrides — they activate at that width and above.

/* This is mobile-first */
class="text-base md:text-lg lg:text-xl"

/* text-base: applies everywhere (mobile baseline)
   md:text-lg: overrides at ≥768px
   lg:text-xl: overrides at ≥1024px */

Write the mobile layout first. Add breakpoint prefixes only where the design needs to change.

The five breakpoints

sm:   ≥ 640px   — large phone / landscape
md:   ≥ 768px   — tablet
lg:   ≥ 1024px  — laptop
xl:   ≥ 1280px  — desktop
2xl:  ≥ 1536px  — large desktop / wide

You don't have to use all five. Most projects use only md: and lg: for the majority of breakpoints.

Responsive grid columns

class="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 gap-6"

/* Mobile:  1 column (stacked)
   ≥640px:  2 columns
   ≥1024px: 3 columns */

This single class string replaces three separate media queries. It's one of the most common patterns in any React UI codebase.

Responsive flex direction

class="flex flex-col md:flex-row gap-6"

/* Mobile: items stack vertically
   Tablet+: items flow horizontally */

A very common pattern for hero sections: content stacks on mobile (text above image), sits side by side on larger screens.

Hiding and showing elements

hidden sm:block      /* hidden on mobile, visible from sm up */
block sm:hidden      /* visible on mobile, hidden from sm up */
hidden md:flex       /* hidden on mobile, flex from md up */

Use this to swap a mobile hamburger menu for a desktop nav link list, without duplicating markup.

Responsive spacing and typography

/* Hero title */
class="text-3xl md:text-5xl lg:text-7xl font-bold"

/* Section padding */
class="py-12 md:py-20 lg:py-32 px-4 md:px-8 lg:px-16"

The container utility

class="container mx-auto px-4"

/* container: sets max-width matching each breakpoint
   mx-auto:   centres horizontally
   px-4:      prevents content from touching the edge on mobile */

Use container mx-auto px-4 on page-level wrapper divs. You almost always want the horizontal padding too.

The common mistake — desktop-first undoing

/* WRONG: desktop-first, trying to undo on mobile */
class="grid-cols-3 sm:grid-cols-1"

/* RIGHT: mobile-first, progressively enhance */
class="grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3"

The mistake is starting with the desktop layout and trying to override it for mobile. Tailwind breakpoints are min-width, so there is no way to say "only below this size" without reaching for the max-md: variant (which exists but is generally a sign of inverted thinking). Write mobile first.

In React/JSX

/* Responsive hero section */
<section className="py-12 md:py-24 px-4">
  <div className="container mx-auto">
    <div className="flex flex-col md:flex-row gap-8 items-center">
      <div className="flex-1">
        <h1 className="text-4xl md:text-6xl font-bold">Heading</h1>
        <p className="mt-4 text-lg text-gray-600">Subheading</p>
      </div>
      <div className="flex-1">
        <img className="rounded-xl w-full" src="..." alt="" />
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain mobile-first in your own words. Why does Tailwind use min-width breakpoints rather than max-width? What goes wrong when developers write desktop-first CSS and try to override it for mobile?

questions.questionHtml: At what minimum viewport width does the md: breakpoint activate?
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's default breakpoints: sm = 640px, md = 768px, lg = 1024px, xl = 1280px, 2xl = 1536px.

questions.questionHtml: What does hidden md:flex mean?
options: Hidden on all screens, flex on md and up
Flex on all screens, hidden on md and up
Hidden below md, flex on md and above
questions.correctAnswer: Hidden below md, flex on md and above
questions.explanationHtml: hidden sets display: none at all sizes (the mobile baseline). md:flex overrides it to display: flex at 768px and above. Together they create a show/hide on breakpoint pattern.

questions.questionHtml: You need cards to stack in a single column on mobile, show 2 columns on tablet, and 4 columns on desktop. Which class string is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: Mobile-first: start with the single-column base (no prefix), then enhance at each breakpoint. The first option correctly uses unprefixed grid-cols-1 as the mobile baseline.

questions.questionHtml: The container utility in Tailwind automatically centres itself horizontally.
questions.explanationHtml: container only sets the max-width to match the current breakpoint. You must also add mx-auto to centre it. The common pattern is always container mx-auto px-4.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes class="grid-cols-3 sm:grid-cols-2 xs:grid-cols-1" to make a grid that shows 1 column on very small screens. There are two bugs. What are they?
questions.correctAnswer: Bug 1: Tailwind has no xs: breakpoint by default — this class is invalid and does nothing. Bug 2: The logic is inverted (desktop-first) — grid-cols-3 is the unprefixed base so it applies to all sizes including mobile. The correct mobile-first approach is grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3.
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's breakpoints start at sm (640px) — there is no xs in the default config. More importantly, because breakpoints are minimum-width, you cannot use them to target small screens. Unprefixed utilities are the mobile baseline; breakpoint prefixes progressively enhance for larger screens.

subChunks.title: State Variants
subChunks.hookHtml: A form input that looks identical whether focused or blurred is a usability failure. A button with no hover state feels like a static image. State variants let you apply utilities only when an element is in a specific condition — hover, focus, disabled, checked, even when a parent or sibling is in a certain state.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The core interactive states

hover:bg-blue-700        /* pointer is over the element */
focus:ring-2             /* element has focus (any method) */
focus-visible:ring-2     /* element focused via KEYBOARD only */
active:scale-95          /* element is being pressed/clicked */
disabled:opacity-50      /* element has disabled attribute */
checked:bg-blue-600      /* checkbox/radio is checked */

focus vs focus-visible — the accessible distinction

focus: fires when the element receives focus by any means — mouse click, keyboard Tab, or programmatic focus. This is often too aggressive: a mouse user doesn't need to see a focus ring after clicking a button (they can see where they just clicked).

focus-visible: only fires when the browser determines the user is navigating by keyboard. This is the correct choice for focus rings on buttons and links — it keeps the UI clean for mouse users while fully supporting keyboard navigation.

/* Accessible button focus ring */
class="focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500 focus-visible:ring-offset-2"

/* Input fields: use focus: here because ALL focus should be visible */
class="focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500 focus:border-blue-500"

Placeholder and form validation states

placeholder:text-gray-400       /* style the placeholder text */
placeholder:italic

required:border-red-300         /* element has required attribute */
invalid:border-red-500          /* element fails HTML5 validation */
valid:border-green-500          /* element passes HTML5 validation */

Parent state — group

Add group to a parent element. Children can then use group-hover:, group-focus:, and more to react to the parent's state.

<div class="group cursor-pointer">
  <h3 class="group-hover:text-blue-600 transition-colors">Title</h3>
  <p class="group-hover:text-gray-900 text-gray-500 transition-colors">Body</p>
  <span class="opacity-0 group-hover:opacity-100 transition-opacity">→</span>
</div>

This pattern is essential for card hover effects where multiple child elements all need to change together.

Sibling state — peer

Add peer to an element. A following sibling can then react to its state with peer-checked:, peer-focus:, peer-placeholder-shown:, and others.

/* Floating label pattern */
<div class="relative">
  <input class="peer w-full pt-6 pb-2 px-3 border rounded-md" placeholder=" " />
  <label class="absolute left-3 top-4 text-gray-500 text-sm
               peer-focus:top-1 peer-focus:text-xs peer-focus:text-blue-600
               peer-placeholder-shown:top-4 peer-placeholder-shown:text-sm
               transition-all">
    Email
  </label>
</div>

List and structural variants

first:rounded-t-lg    /* applies only to the first child */
last:rounded-b-lg     /* applies only to the last child */
odd:bg-gray-50        /* every odd-numbered child */
even:bg-white         /* every even-numbered child */

Disabled state in React — replacing conditional class logic

In React codebases, developers often write:

/* The old way — conditional className logic */
<button
  className={`px-4 py-2 rounded ${isLoading ? 'opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed' : 'hover:bg-blue-700'}`}
  disabled={isLoading}
>

/* The Tailwind way — let CSS handle it */
<button
  className="px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700
             disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed
             transition-colors"
  disabled={isLoading}
>

The disabled: variant reads the actual DOM disabled attribute. When the attribute is present, the utility fires automatically — no JavaScript class toggling required.

ARIA state variants

aria-checked:bg-blue-600    /* element has aria-checked="true" */
aria-expanded:rotate-180    /* element has aria-expanded="true" */
aria-disabled:opacity-50    /* element has aria-disabled="true" */

These are particularly useful for custom interactive components (accordions, dropdowns) that communicate state through ARIA attributes rather than native HTML states.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between focus: and focus-visible: variants. When would you use each one, and why does the distinction matter for accessibility?

questions.questionHtml: Which variant applies a utility only when the element receives keyboard focus (not mouse click)?
questions.explanationHtml: focus-visible: maps to the CSS :focus-visible pseudo-class, which the browser only activates when it determines the user is navigating by keyboard. This is the correct choice for focus rings on interactive elements.

questions.questionHtml: Which class applies when the element has the HTML disabled attribute present?
questions.explanationHtml: The disabled: variant reads the native HTML disabled attribute directly from the DOM. When present, the variant's utilities are applied automatically — no JavaScript class manipulation needed.

questions.questionHtml: You have a card that should darken its title and reveal a hidden arrow when the entire card is hovered. What is the correct Tailwind approach?
options: Add group to the card, use group-hover: on the title and arrow
Add hover: to both the title and the arrow individually
Use JavaScript to add/remove classes on mouseover
Use peer on the card and peer-hover: on children
questions.correctAnswer: Add group to the card, use group-hover: on the title and arrow
questions.explanationHtml: The group + group-hover: pattern is precisely designed for this: add group to the parent, and any descendant can react to the parent's hover state with group-hover: variants. peer is for sibling relationships, not parent-child.

questions.questionHtml: In React, you can use disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed on a button and simply set the disabled prop — without writing any conditional className JavaScript for those visual states.
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's disabled: variant reads the actual DOM disabled attribute. When you pass disabled as a React prop, it sets the attribute on the DOM element, which Tailwind's CSS selector :disabled picks up automatically.

questions.questionHtml: A developer styles a custom toggle component using checked:bg-blue-600 on a <div> element. The toggle's checked state is tracked in React state and toggled with an onClick handler, but the checked: variant never applies. Why doesn't it work, and what is the correct approach?
questions.correctAnswer: The checked: variant targets the native CSS :checked pseudo-class, which only applies to actual form inputs (checkbox, radio). A div never has a :checked state. For a custom toggle, either use a visually-hidden checkbox underneath (which can use checked:), or use aria-checked attribute and the aria-checked: variant, or drive the appearance purely from React state with a conditional class.
questions.explanationHtml: CSS pseudo-classes like :checked, :disabled, and :required only fire on native HTML form elements that have those states. A custom <div>-based component has no native checked state. The solutions are: (1) use an actual hidden <input type="checkbox"> with peer to drive sibling styling, (2) use aria-checked with the aria-checked: variant, or (3) pass the state via a data attribute and style with arbitrary variants.

subChunks.title: Dark Mode
subChunks.hookHtml: Dark mode is no longer a novelty feature — users expect it, and many accessibility needs depend on it. Tailwind's dark: variant lets you specify dark-mode styles inline with your light-mode classes, with no separate stylesheet required.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Two strategies for enabling dark mode

// tailwind.config.js

// Strategy 1: follow OS preference
darkMode: 'media'

// Strategy 2: manual toggle via a class on html element
darkMode: 'class'

The 'media' strategy uses the prefers-color-scheme: dark media query — dark mode turns on automatically when the user's OS is in dark mode. The 'class' strategy turns on dark mode when the HTML element has a dark class.

For production apps, use 'class'. It lets users choose a preference independent of their OS setting, which is the expectation most users have. The 'media' strategy is easier to set up but removes user control.

Applying dark: styles

<div class="bg-white dark:bg-gray-900
            text-gray-900 dark:text-white
            border border-gray-200 dark:border-gray-700">
  Content
</div>

Unprefixed = light mode. dark: prefix = dark mode override. You typically only need dark variants for colour-related utilities — spacing, typography sizes, and layout utilities stay the same.

Common dark mode colour mappings

Light                   →  Dark
bg-white                →  dark:bg-gray-900
bg-gray-50              →  dark:bg-gray-800
bg-gray-100             →  dark:bg-gray-700
text-gray-900           →  dark:text-white
text-gray-700           →  dark:text-gray-200
text-gray-500           →  dark:text-gray-400
border-gray-200         →  dark:border-gray-700
bg-blue-100 text-blue-800 →  dark:bg-blue-900/30 dark:text-blue-400

The pattern: light backgrounds invert to dark backgrounds (gray-900, gray-800). Light text inverts to lighter text. Border colours get darker. Coloured tags use low-opacity backgrounds in dark mode.

Toggling dark mode in React

// A minimal dark mode toggle
function ThemeToggle() {
  const [dark, setDark] = useState(
    () => localStorage.getItem('theme') === 'dark'
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark);
    localStorage.setItem('theme', dark ? 'dark' : 'light');
  }, [dark]);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setDark(d => !d)}>
      {dark ? '☀️ Light' : '🌙 Dark'}
    </button>
  );
}

The key line is document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark) — this adds or removes the dark class from the <html> element, which is what darkMode: 'class' watches.

Dark mode with opacity modifiers

dark:bg-blue-900/30    /* blue-900 at 30% opacity */
dark:text-white/80     /* white at 80% opacity */

The slash opacity modifier works with any colour utility including dark-prefixed ones. Particularly useful for subtle dark-mode accent backgrounds.

Stacking dark with other variants

dark:hover:bg-gray-700    /* dark mode AND hovered */
dark:focus:ring-gray-500  /* dark mode AND focused */
dark:md:text-xl           /* dark mode AND md+ screen */

What you still need to handle

Tailwind's dark: variant handles CSS. You still need to:

  • Read the user's saved preference from localStorage on page load
  • Avoid the flash of wrong theme on initial render (set the class in a blocking script before React hydrates)
  • Persist the preference
/* In public/index.html — before React loads */
<script>
  if (localStorage.theme === 'dark' ||
      (!('theme' in localStorage) &&
       window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches)) {
    document.documentElement.classList.add('dark')
  }
</script>

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between darkMode: 'media' and darkMode: 'class' in tailwind.config.js. When would you choose each, and what does adding the dark class to the html element actually do?

questions.questionHtml: Which config value enables dark mode by adding a dark class to the <html> element?
questions.explanationHtml: darkMode: 'class' tells Tailwind to activate dark mode utilities when the dark class is present on the root element. Your JavaScript is responsible for toggling that class.

questions.questionHtml: Which class correctly pairs a white light background with a gray-900 dark background?
questions.explanationHtml: Unprefixed = light mode baseline. dark: prefix = override when dark mode is active. The combination bg-white dark:bg-gray-900 is the canonical inverted background pattern.

questions.questionHtml: You want a blue badge that uses a subtle dark background in dark mode — not a solid dark-blue block, but a tinted wash. Which dark mode class achieves this?
questions.explanationHtml: The slash opacity modifier (/30) reduces the background to 30% opacity, creating a subtle tint. dark:bg-blue-900/30 is the standard pattern for coloured badges in dark mode — solid blue-900 is too heavy and looks like a block, while 30% opacity reads as a tag colour.

questions.questionHtml: With darkMode: 'media', users who prefer light mode in their OS settings cannot override the app to show dark mode.
questions.explanationHtml: darkMode: 'media' is entirely driven by the OS prefers-color-scheme media query. There is no way for an in-app toggle to override it — the app always follows the OS setting. This is why darkMode: 'class' is preferred for apps that want to give users explicit control.

questions.questionHtml: A developer sets up darkMode: 'class' and adds a React toggle button that calls document.body.classList.toggle('dark'). They apply dark:bg-gray-900 to the page wrapper but it never activates. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: The dark class must be added to the html element (document.documentElement), not the body element. Tailwind's class strategy looks for the dark class on the root html element, not on body or any other element.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the most common dark mode implementation mistake. Tailwind's darkMode: 'class' generates CSS selectors like .dark .dark\:bg-gray-900 which require dark to be an ancestor class. By convention and by Tailwind's implementation, this ancestor is the <html> element (document.documentElement). The fix is document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark').

subChunks.title: Transitions & Animations
subChunks.hookHtml: The difference between a UI that feels polished and one that feels cheap is often just a 150ms transition. Without one, hover states snap, buttons teleport, and modals pop in jarringly. Tailwind provides transition, duration, and easing utilities — plus four built-in animations for common patterns like loading states and notification indicators.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The fundamental rule of transitions

The transition utility goes on the base state, not the hover state. This is a common mistake.

/* WRONG — transition on the hover state */
class="bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 hover:transition-colors"

/* CORRECT — transition on the base, hover changes the property */
class="bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 transition-colors duration-150"

Why? The transition needs to apply in both directions — when the state activates and when it deactivates (mouse-out). If you put the transition on hover:, the forward transition works but the reverse snap is instant.

Transition utilities

transition            /* transition: all properties that commonly animate */
transition-colors     /* only color, bg, border, fill, stroke */
transition-transform  /* only transform */
transition-opacity    /* only opacity */
transition-shadow     /* only box-shadow */
transition-none       /* disable all transitions */

Prefer transition-colors for buttons and links — it only transitions colour properties, which is more performant than transition. Prefer transition-transform for scale/rotate effects.

Duration and easing

duration-75    /* 75ms  — near-instant */
duration-100   /* 100ms — fast */
duration-150   /* 150ms — the standard for interactive UI */
duration-200   /* 200ms */
duration-300   /* 300ms — modals, panels opening */
duration-500   /* 500ms — hero transitions */

ease-linear    /* constant speed */
ease-in        /* slow start, fast end */
ease-out       /* fast start, slow end (natural for things entering) */
ease-in-out    /* slow start, slow end (natural for transitions) */

For most interactive states (button hover, link hover): duration-150 ease-in-out. For UI panels entering the screen: duration-200 ease-out.

Transform utilities

scale-95       /* 95% — pressed/active state */
scale-100      /* 100% — default */
scale-105      /* 105% — hovered card lift */
rotate-45      /* 45 degree rotation */
rotate-180     /* 180 degrees — accordion arrow */
-translate-y-1 /* shift up 4px — subtle card lift */
translate-x-full /* shift fully right — slide out */

Built-in animations

animate-spin    /* 360deg rotation loop — loading spinners */
animate-pulse   /* opacity 0.5 ↔ 1 loop — skeleton loading screens */
animate-bounce  /* bouncing Y-axis — scroll indicators */
animate-ping    /* scale 1→2 with opacity fade — notification dots */

Combining them — practical examples

/* Primary button with all interactive states */
class="bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 active:scale-95
       transition-all duration-150 ease-in-out
       motion-reduce:transition-none"

/* Loading spinner */
<svg class="animate-spin h-5 w-5 text-white" ...>

/* Skeleton loading line */
<div class="h-4 bg-gray-200 rounded animate-pulse"></div>

/* Notification badge */
<span class="relative flex h-2 w-2">
  <span class="animate-ping absolute inline-flex h-full w-full rounded-full bg-red-400 opacity-75"></span>
  <span class="relative inline-flex rounded-full h-2 w-2 bg-red-500"></span>
</span>

/* Accordion arrow that rotates open */
<svg class="rotate-0 group-open:rotate-180 transition-transform duration-200">

Accessibility — ALWAYS add reduced motion

Some users experience nausea, dizziness, or seizure risk from motion. The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets them opt out of animations. Tailwind provides two variants:

motion-safe:animate-bounce     /* only animates if user HASN'T requested reduced motion */
motion-reduce:transition-none  /* disables transition if user HAS requested reduced motion */
motion-reduce:animate-none     /* disables animation if user HAS requested reduced motion */

For any attention-grabbing or looping animation, always add motion-safe: or motion-reduce:animate-none. For transitions on interactive elements, add motion-reduce:transition-none. This is a WCAG requirement and a mark of professional work.

storyBeats.text: Sable presses a finger to a rune on the door. It doesn't snap to lit — it breathes into it, steady over a single heartbeat.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: The snap is cheap. The breath is craft. One hundred and fifty milliseconds, ease-in-out — that is the difference between a button that feels alive and one that feels painted on a wall.

storyBeats.speaker: Transition on the base state (correct)
storyBeats.text:
<!-- CORRECT: transition on the element, hover changes the value -->
<button class="bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 active:scale-95
              transition-all duration-150 ease-in-out
              motion-reduce:transition-none">
  Submit
</button>

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: And remember — motion-reduce:transition-none. Always. Some readers cannot tolerate motion. Ignoring them is not craft. It is negligence.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build an animated interactive button and a skeleton loading card.

  • .btn-primary: inline-flex, items-center, gap-2, px-5, py-2.5, bg-blue-600, hover:bg-blue-700, active:scale-95, text-white, text-sm, font-medium, rounded-lg, transition-all, duration-150, ease-in-out, motion-reduce:transition-none
  • .spinner: animate-spin, h-4, w-4
  • .skeleton-line: h-4, bg-gray-200, rounded, animate-pulse
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why does the transition utility need to be on the base state rather than the hover state? What happens to the transition if you put it only on hover:? Also explain why motion-reduce:transition-none matters.

questions.questionHtml: Which animation class creates a repeating scale-and-fade effect, commonly used for notification dot indicators?
questions.explanationHtml: animate-ping scales an element up while fading it out, creating a ripple/radar effect. It's the standard pattern for the pulsing notification dot. animate-pulse is for skeleton loading screens, animate-spin for spinners, and animate-bounce for vertical bouncing.

questions.questionHtml: Which transition class only animates colour-related properties (background, text color, border color) — not all properties?
questions.explanationHtml: transition-colors limits the CSS transition to color, background-color, border-color, text-decoration-color, fill, stroke. This is more performant than transition (which transitions everything) and avoids accidental transitions on layout properties.

questions.questionHtml: A loading indicator is an SVG that should spin continuously. Which class produces this effect?
questions.explanationHtml: animate-spin applies a continuous 360-degree rotation animation. It is the standard class for loading spinners in Tailwind.

questions.questionHtml: motion-reduce:transition-none removes transitions for users who have enabled the "reduce motion" accessibility setting in their operating system.
questions.explanationHtml: motion-reduce: targets the CSS media query prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, which is set by the user in OS accessibility settings (macOS: Reduce Motion, Windows: Turn off animations). Adding motion-reduce:transition-none respects that preference.

questions.questionHtml: A developer applies hover:transition-colors hover:duration-200 hover:bg-blue-700 to a button. When testing, the forward hover transition (light to dark) works, but when the cursor leaves, the background snaps back instantly instead of transitioning. What is the bug?
questions.correctAnswer: The transition utilities are on the hover state, so they only apply when the element is hovered. When the cursor leaves, the hover state is removed — taking the transition with it — so the reverse change is instant. The fix is to put transition-colors and duration-200 on the base element, not under hover:.
questions.explanationHtml: CSS transitions must be present on the element in both states for the transition to work in both directions. If transition-colors is only under hover:, the browser adds the transition when the mouse enters (forward works) but removes it when the mouse leaves (reverse snaps). Moving transition-colors duration-200 to the base class fixes both directions.

subChunks.title: Component Extraction & Reuse
subChunks.hookHtml: At some point, you'll have a button with fifteen utility classes repeated in six files. When the designer changes the border radius, you'll have to update it in all six places. This chunk covers the three strategies for managing repetition in a Tailwind codebase — and crucially, which one is right in which situation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The three strategies

When you have the same set of utility classes appearing in multiple places, you have three options:

  1. React components — extract a <Button> component. The classes live in JSX. This is the correct approach in 95% of cases.
  2. @apply — create a CSS class that bundles utilities. Use this only for styles on HTML you don't control (markdown output, third-party widgets).
  3. Multi-cursor editing — if you have 2–3 identical elements in one file, just edit them all at once. Not a scalable strategy.

Strategy 1: React components — the right approach

/* BEFORE: classes repeated across many files */
<button className="inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700
                   text-white text-sm font-medium rounded-md transition-colors
                   disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed">
  Submit
</button>

/* AFTER: extract a Button component */
function Button({ children, variant = 'primary', ...props }) {
  const base = 'inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium rounded-md transition-colors disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed';
  const variants = {
    primary: 'bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white',
    secondary: 'bg-white hover:bg-gray-50 text-gray-900 border border-gray-300',
    ghost: 'bg-transparent hover:bg-gray-100 text-gray-700',
  };
  return <button className={`${base} ${variants[variant]}`} {...props}>{children}</button>;
}

The classes still live in JSX. Tailwind can still scan them. The component provides a single place to update.

Strategy 2: @apply — use sparingly

/* index.css */
@layer components {
  .btn-primary {
    @apply inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700
           text-white text-sm font-medium rounded-md transition-colors;
  }
}

When to use @apply:

  • Styling HTML you don't write (a markdown renderer outputs plain <p> and <h2> tags you can't add classes to)
  • A third-party widget you're skinning
  • Global base styles for HTML elements

When NOT to use @apply:

  • React, Vue, or Svelte components — use a component instead
  • As a crutch for avoiding learning component composition
  • At scale with modifier classes — this recreates BEM and you lose all of Tailwind's benefits

The extraction rule

Don't extract until you have the same styles in 3+ places that you can't solve with a loop or a component. Premature abstraction makes refactoring harder, not easier.

/* If you have this in ONE file — don't extract */
{items.map(item => (
  <div key={item.id} className="bg-white p-4 rounded-lg shadow-sm">
    {item.name}
  </div>
))}
/* ^ This is already DRY. The className appears once, rendered many times. */

A first taste of cn() — conditional class composition

In production React + Tailwind codebases, you'll encounter a utility function called cn(). It combines clsx (conditional classes) with tailwind-merge (deduplication when classes conflict).

import { clsx } from 'clsx';
import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

function cn(...inputs) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs));
}

/* Usage in a Button component */
function Button({ className, variant = 'primary', ...props }) {
  return (
    <button
      className={cn(
        'inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 rounded-md font-medium text-sm transition-colors',
        variant === 'primary' && 'bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white',
        variant === 'secondary' && 'bg-white border border-gray-300 hover:bg-gray-50',
        className  // allow callers to extend/override
      )}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}

The twMerge part is critical: if a caller passes className="bg-red-600", tailwind-merge removes bg-blue-600 from the base, preventing conflicting background classes from stacking. Deep coverage of CVA and cn() patterns is in the Expert tier.

Tailwind v4 — a brief heads-up

Tailwind v4 moves to a CSS-first configuration. Instead of tailwind.config.js, you import Tailwind directly:

/* v4 approach */
@import "tailwindcss";
@theme {
  --color-brand: #6d28d9;
}

The utility class API stays the same. If you encounter a codebase using @import "tailwindcss" at the top of a CSS file instead of @tailwind base/components/utilities, that's a v4 project.

storyBeats.text: Maester Cordell holds up two scrolls — one dense with repeated incantations, one compact with named spells. Both achieve the same result. Only one scales.

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: When the same utility string appears in three places, you have a decision. In a React project, the answer is almost always the same: make a component. The classes stay in JSX where Tailwind can find them. The abstraction lives where abstractions belong — in the language.

storyBeats.speaker: Button component (the right approach)
Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: @apply has its place — when you're styling HTML you didn't write. A markdown renderer's output. A third-party widget. Not your own React components. Reach for @apply there and you've rebuilt BEM on top of Tailwind. That is not a trade worth making.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a button system showing three variants by applying the correct classes to each button type.

  • All .btn-base elements share: inline-flex, items-center, px-4, py-2, rounded-md, font-medium, text-sm, transition-colors, duration-150
  • .btn-primary adds: bg-blue-600, hover:bg-blue-700, text-white

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three approaches to managing repeated utility classes in a Tailwind codebase. When is each one appropriate? Why does the Tailwind team recommend components over @apply for React projects?

questions.questionHtml: In which CSS layer should @apply component classes be defined to ensure correct specificity ordering?
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's three layers in order are base, components, utilities. Component classes belong in @layer components so that utility classes (in @layer utilities) can still override them with higher specificity.

questions.questionHtml: What does tailwind-merge solve that plain clsx does not?
options: Removes conflicting Tailwind classes (e.g. two bg- classes)
Adds TypeScript types to className strings
Generates class names at build time
questions.correctAnswer: Removes conflicting Tailwind classes (e.g. two bg- classes)
questions.explanationHtml: clsx only handles conditional inclusion of class strings — it doesn't know anything about Tailwind. If you end up with both bg-blue-600 and bg-red-600, clsx passes both through and CSS specificity determines which wins (unpredictably). tailwind-merge understands Tailwind's class groups and removes the conflicting class, keeping only the last one.

questions.questionHtml: You're building a React app and your card component appears in 20 places with identical styling. What is the correct approach?
options: Extract a Card React component with the classes in JSX
Create a .card class with @apply in your CSS file
Use CSS variables to parameterise the classes
Repeat the classes each time — that is the Tailwind way
questions.correctAnswer: Extract a Card React component with the classes in JSX
questions.explanationHtml: In a component-based framework, the component IS the abstraction. Extract a <Card> component and keep the Tailwind classes in JSX. This keeps Tailwind's scanning working correctly, co-locates styles with markup, and provides a single source of truth to update.

questions.questionHtml: In a React project, using @apply to create a .btn-primary CSS class is generally preferable to extracting a <Button> React component.
questions.explanationHtml: The Tailwind team explicitly recommends the opposite. In React (and Vue/Svelte), the component IS the reuse mechanism. @apply fights against how Tailwind is designed to work — it recreates traditional CSS class authoring and loses the benefits of utility composition. Use @apply only for HTML you don't control (markdown output, third-party widgets).

questions.questionHtml: A team heavily uses @apply for all their components over six months: .card, .btn, .badge, .modal, with modifier classes like .btn-sm, .btn-danger, .card-featured. They now have 40+ component classes with modifier variants. What problem have they created, and what should they have done instead?
questions.correctAnswer: They've rebuilt a traditional CSS component library (essentially BEM) on top of Tailwind, losing all of Tailwind's composition advantages. They now have the complexity of maintaining both a utility system and a component class system. The fix is to use React components with props for variants — a Button component that accepts a variant prop ('primary' | 'danger' | 'sm') keeps the classes in JSX and composes cleanly without accumulating CSS.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the most common Tailwind anti-pattern in team codebases. The @apply approach feels familiar to developers with a CSS background, but it reintroduces all the problems Tailwind was designed to solve: styles in separate files from markup, unclear relationships between classes, specificity conflicts, and growing CSS file size. Component + CVA (or a simple variants map) is the scalable solution.
